destination.title: He warned regulators about Madoff for nearly ten years

short05: For decades, he paid steady profits.
In reality, he was barely investing the money at all.
His was one of the most trusted names on Wall Street, with smooth, steady returns year after year.
But investigators found there were almost no real trades.
The profits were just new investors' money handed to old ones.
It collapsed in 2008, and he was sentenced to a hundred and fifty years.
Returns that look too smooth can be the warning sign.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: And for nearly ten years, nobody listened to him.
And in return, he gave them a number that almost never went down.
Here's what almost nobody understood until it was too late: that steadiness wasn't a sign that the money was safe.
If Madoff almost never lost money, in markets that destroyed everyone else… *how?* The answer is that he wasn't really investing the money at all.
Trade confirmations for trades that never happened.
It went up in good times and up in bad times, with almost none of the dips that real markets force on real investors.
Like a player who never, ever loses — not because they're great, but because the game is rigged.
The man who'd solved it sat outside, watching the largest fraud in history continue in plain sight, because the people with the power to stop it never did the math.
Its finding was not that the agency was corrupt — there's no evidence anyone was paid off.
The finding was, in some ways, worse: they had received credible, specific warnings, for years, and simply never ran them down properly.
In December 2008, Madoff told his sons the truth — that the business was, in his own words, one big lie.
A few months later, in March 2009, Madoff stood in a federal courtroom in New York and pleaded guilty — not to one charge, but to eleven felonies.
